newsitem.title: USA: Late-planted US oat crop vulnerable to summer heat.
newsitem.headline: Late-planted US oat crop vulnerable to summer heat.

text.p: Temperatures in June and early July will determine the fate of the late-planted U.S. oat crop, agronomists and crop watchers said.

"If temperatures turn hot in June, things could be damaged quite a bit," said Mike Peel, crop specialist with North Dakota State University. "We don't have any (weather) guarantees and the potential exists for damage."
Flooding, heavy rains and late spring snow storms significantly delayed the planting of the oat crop in northern Plains states and Minnesota.
Oat plants in the more advanced boot and heading stages flourish in cool weather, so a late planting leaves plants more susceptible to damage from the summer's high temperatures, agronomists said.
Ninety-degree Fahrenheit temperatures during the day and eighty-degree readings at night when the plants are in the heading stage can significantly reduce test weights, agronomists said.
Bob Hall, crop specialist with South Dakota State University estimated that state's crop was planted at least a month late.
"Our recommendation is that you have most of your small grains planted by the 20th of April," Hall said. "After that, you start getting some yield reductions."
In North and South Dakota, oat plantings accelerated in the last week, but crop emergence still lags behind the average pace.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported oat emergence as of Sunday in North Dakota was 35 percent behind the five-year average of 52 percent. In South Dakota, emergence was 55 percent versus 77 percent on average.

In Minnesota, the crop is behind average pace in both plantings and emergence. Oats there were 89 percent planted versus the average pace of 94 percent, and 71 percent of the crop was emerged, lagging the five-year average of 82 percent.

"The biggest concern here would be the late plantings," said Kent Thiesse, a state crop specialist in southwestern Minnesota. "In the flooded areas like the Red River Valley, a lot of the small grains were not planted until May."
Typically, Minnesota oats are planted in mid-April, Thiesse said.

Much-below-normal temperatures this spring were also seen an impediment to the development of the oat crop in Minnesota. The young plants need heat during emergence and early development, but the number of growing degree days in this year have been reduced by 40 to 50 percent, Thiesse said.
"The cooler temps may have been a detriment rather than a help because they're coming at the wrong time," Thiesse said.
In the Dakotas, cool weather has also hindered crop development by slowing emergence, agronmists said.
"We've not had real good weather yet," Hall said. "There's a lot of seed in the ground that's just been sitting there because it's too cold," Hall said.
